opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it wasn't that Google was a bad place. It's an amazing company with incredible people. But when I thought about what I actually wanted to do day to day, a few things didn't fit.

The biggest one is scale versus impact. At a huge company, you're often one small piece of a very large machine. You might spend months optimizing something that moves a metric by a fraction of a percent, and that can be meaningful, but I wanted to feel that my work directly changed the outcome. I wanted to be in a place where, if I didn't do something, it just wouldn't happen.

The second is speed. Big companies naturally have more process: reviews, approvals, coordination across teams. That exists for good reasons, but I'm someone who likes to build quickly, try things, break things, and iterate. When I worked on open-source projects like Tianshou, I could go from an idea to working code in a day or two. I didn't want to lose that feeling.

And third, I wanted to work on something at the frontier, where the problems are still open and nobody really knows the answer yet. At a smaller, more focused organization, you're much closer to that edge. You're figuring things out as you go, and you're surrounded by people who are all pushing in the same direction.

So it was less about Google being unappealing and more about knowing what kind of environment brings out the best in me.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that at a huge company you are often “one small piece of a very large machine,” conveying the expected cog-like role.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't that Google was unappealing in itself. It's a great place with incredibly smart people. It was more about what I wanted out of my own time.

I'm the kind of person who likes to build things end to end. I did Tianshou, the reinforcement learning library, mostly on my own at first, and what I loved was that I could decide the design, write the code, talk to users, and ship a fix the same day. At a very large company, the systems are so mature that a lot of the work is about fitting into them. You own a small slice, and the path from an idea to something real can go through many layers of review and planning. That's the right thing for a company at that scale, but for me it felt like the feedback loop was too slow.

The other piece was the type of problem. I wanted to be close to the frontier where things are still messy and undecided, where the infrastructure doesn't exist yet and you have to invent it. That's where I think I learn the fastest, and where an individual can still have an outsized impact. At a big company, those messy problems tend to get carved up before they reach you.

So it was less a judgment about Google and more about knowing myself. I'd rather be at a place where if something is broken, I can just go fix it tonight.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that at a very large company they would own only a small slice and fit into mature systems, with messy problems divided up before reaching them. This conveys the expectation of becoming a small cog in a larger organization.

I was more drawn to building something from the beginning, making decisions, and seeing directly whether those decisions worked. That uncertainty felt more exciting to me than having a clearly defined path.
